newsitem.title: ARMENIA: IMF says slow-reform Armenia risks loan delay.
newsitem.headline: IMF says slow-reform Armenia risks loan delay.

text.p: Armenia is in danger of losing vital credits from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) because of tax collection problems and slow reform of its banking system, an IMF official said on Friday.

Thanos Catsambas, head of an IMF delegation winding up a visit to the capital Yerevan, gave the government until March 15 to improve its record in these two areas and said that otherwise the next tranche of a $50 million loan for 1997 would be delayed.

"There are two or three most important (conditions) that the government has not completed as it promised. We sincerely hope it will be able to implement these reforms," he told Reuters in an interview.

Catsambas said the IMF was still not satisfied with the government's efforts to collect taxes from delinquent state and private enterprises. He said this made revenues projected under the recently adopted 1997 budget "overly optimistic."
He also said reform of the banking sector was too slow.

"If these problems are not rectified, then there will definitely be serious problems for our presentation of the Armenian programme," he said, referring to a report due from the delegation to the IMF Board of Directors.
Catsambas, although emphasizing that Armenia had made "great progress" in overall reforms since independence in 1991, said that if the conditions were not met in time, the credit would be delayed.
The $50 million loan is part of a three-year, $150 million programme.

Armenia, a landlocked country of three and a half million, has recorded impressive economic statistics over the past two years despite a long, debilitating conflict with neighbour Azerbaijan over territory.

The government said last week it expected 1996 yearly inflation of just 5.7 percent, one of the lowest figures in the post-Soviet Commonwealth of Independent States. Official final figures are to be released next month.
Industrial production has also soared since the beginning of 1996.
Despite this most Armenians are still poor and average monthly wages hover only around $20 per month.
